items.summary: बीते अगस्त में न्यूज़लॉन्ड्री ने एक रिपोर्ट की थी. इसमें सामने आया था कि उत्तराखंड में मतदाता सूचियों के विशेष गहन पुनरीक्षण (एसआईआर) के दौरान थोक फॉर्म-7 आवेदनों के ज़रिये मतदाताओं को निशाना बनाया जा रहा है. राज्य के कई विधानसभा क्षेत्रों में भाजपा कार्यकर्ताओं ने हज़ारों फॉर्म-7 आवेदन दाखिल किए. इनमें ज़्यादातर आपत्तियां मुस्लिम मतदाताओं के ख़िलाफ थीं. उधम सिंह नगर जिले की किच्छा विधानसभा में 6,884 फॉर्म-7 आपत्तियों दर्ज हुई जिसमें से 5,359 राजेश तिवारी ने की थीं. तिवारी भाजपा से जुड़े बूथ लेवल एजेंट (बीएलए) हैं. वह पूर्व विधायक राजेश शुक्ला के करीबी और उधम सिंह नगर में भाजपा के जिला प्रकोष्ठ संयोजक हैं. पूरे उत्तराखंड में सबसे ज़्यादा फॉर्म-7 आपत्तियां इन्होंने ही दाखिल कीं. न्यूज़लॉन्ड्री से बातचीत में तिवारी ने दावा किया कि स्थानीय निर्वाचक पंजीकरण अधिकारी (ईआरओ) ने शुरू में थोक फॉर्म-7 आपत्तियां लेने से इनकार कर दिया था. उनके मुताबिक़ ईआरओ का कहना था कि भारत निर्वाचन आयोग (ईसीआई) के नियमों में ऐसा कोई प्रावधान नहीं है. इसके बाद उन्होंने इसीआई को ईमेल कर ईआरओ की शिकायत की और साथ ही अपनी आपत्ति भेजी. न्यूज़लॉन्ड्री इस ईमेल की विषय-वस्तु की स्वतंत्र रूप से पुष्टि नहीं कर सका है. तिवारी ने कहा, “ईमेल भेजने के दो दिन के भीतर ईआरओ कार्यालय से फोन आया और मुझसे आपत्तियां जमा करने को कहा गया.” हमने उत्तराखंड के सीईओ, मुख्य निर्वाचन आयुक्त और दोनों निर्वाचन आयुक्तों, आयोग के मीडिया विभाग को सवाल ईमेल किए, जिसमें तिवारी के इस दावे पर सवाल हैं कि क्या ईसीआई ने ईआरओ को उनकी थोक फॉर्म-7 आपत्तियां स्वीकार करने का निर्देश दिया था. ईसीआई ने हमारा ईमेल प्राप्त होने की पुष्टि की और हमारा फोन नंबर मांगा, लेकिन हमारे सवालों के जवाब नहीं दिए. जवाब मिलने पर हम इस रिपोर्ट को अपडेट करेंगे. किच्छा के ईआरओ गौरव पांडे ने इन दावों की न पुष्टि की, न खंडन. उन्होंने न्यूज़लॉन्ड्री से कहा, “हमारा एसआईआर पूरा हो चुका है. दावे और आपत्तियां हमने सुन ली हैं और वह प्रक्रिया भी समाप्त हो गई है. इसके अलावा मैं इस पर कुछ नहीं कह सकता.” जब पूछा गया कि क्या तिवारी की आपत्तियों पर उन्हें ईसीआई से कोई विशेष निर्देश मिला था, तो उन्होंने कहा, “इस पर मैं कुछ नहीं कह सकता.” उन्होंने यह भी कहा कि यह प्रक्रिया दो महीने पहले हुई थी और उन्हें सारी बातें याद नहीं हैं. नाम हटाए जाने के सवाल पर उन्होंने कहा, “हमने जो भी किया है, वह ईसीआई के नियमों के अनुसार किया है.” उत्तराखंड items.title: South Central 98: Key developments in protests and crackdown in Delhi
items.summary: Were Saurav Das and Ashutosh detained for breaching a peace bond, or were preventive powers being used to restrict their right to protest? In this week’s South Central, hosts Dhanya Rajendran and Pooja Prasanna examine the legal questions surrounding the detention of Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, the use of peace bonds and the limits of the state’s power to prevent protests. They are joined by Apar Gupta, advocate and founder-director of the Internet Freedom Foundation, to discuss the role of executive magistrates, preventive detention and the implications for the right to dissent. The discussion examines how executive magistrates can require people to sign peace bonds to maintain public order, and what happens when authorities subsequently detain them for allegedly violating those conditions. It also looks at the distinction between preventing a possible breach of peace and using preventive powers to restrict people’s freedom to protest. Apar Gupta questions the legality of the detentions, arguing that the authorities’ actions in this case were unlawful and that the two men should have been released. The conversation also explores the powers exercised by executive magistrates, the potential for their misuse, and why legal safeguards are necessary to ensure that measures intended to maintain public order do not become a means of curbing constitutional freedoms. items.title: Legora raises US$550 million from Series E fundraise
items.summary: Legora , the agentic operating system for legal professionals, has raised a US$550 million Series E at a US$8.8 billion post-money valuation. Atreides Management led the round, with new investors including Baron Capital, Capital Group, Fidelity Management & Research Company, Glade Brook Capital Partners, and J.P. Morgan. All major existing investors, including Accel, Benchmark, Bessemer Venture Partners, General Catalyst, ICONIQ, Insight Venture Partners, Redpoint Ventures, Salesforce Ventures, and Sands Capital, are also participating. The raise comes as Legora's adoption grows in India, where customers include leading law firms such as Cyril Amarchand Mangaldas and Veritas Legal, as well as in-house legal teams. Legora has an office in Bengaluru, one of its Asia-Pacific offices alongside Sydney, Singapore, Tokyo, and Seoul, and expects its regional team to reach more than 100 people by the end of 2026. "India's legal market is large, fast-moving and increasingly connected to the rest of the world. Law firms like Cyril Amarchand Mangaldas and in-house teams here are moving from trying AI to relying on it for real work. Bengaluru is part of a team that's growing across Asia-Pacific, and this round means we can keep investing in the people and the product that customers in India depend on," said Heather Paterson , VP of Legora APJ. The round follows a period of rapid growth. Legora went from US$1 million to US$100 million in ARR in less than 18 months, faster than any other enterprise software company selling through a direct sales team, and the next US$100 million took less than six months. ARR now stands at more than US$200 million. The new valuation compares with US$5.6 billion at the company's previous round. "The opportunity in legal is enormous and we are still early. AI is changing the role of the lawyer, with more time for judgement and advice, and it is reshaping how law firms and in-house legal teams are organised and how their work gets done. We intend to lead that shift in the US and globally. We chose investors who share our long-term view and know what it takes to build a lasting company. They are the right partners for the years ahead," said Max Junestrand , CEO and Co-Founder of Legora. The capital will support continued expansion and deepen investment in the Legora aOS, the agentic operating system that lawyers and their agents work in, bringing new products such as agentic intake, horizon scanning and legal research to customers.

In his book, he recounts a discussion called at the behest of then Chief Justice of India (CJI) DY Chandrachud and also involving Justice Sanjiv Khanna , where he was asked to take a "middle path" in the case concerning the validity of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) and reconsideration of the Court's 2022 judgment in Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v. Union of India . Justice Kaul described it as an attempt to "take the case away from him" and that can "only have been done by the Chief Justice himself". This, the book states, "drove a wedge between the Chief Justice and me". As per the book, "One morning, I was called to the CJI's chamber where Justice Khanna also happened to be present along with him and asked "whether I really wished to go on with the matter." It was then put to me that caution must be the wiser course and that perhaps I should take a middle path." Justice Kaul, in his interview to The Wire, further said that while he does not recollect who exactly made the "middle path" suggestion, the line of discussion was whether he should continue hearing the case. "I do not exactly recollect whether it was him (CJI Chandrachud) or Justice Khanna but that was the line of discussion - whether I would like to go on with the matter." He added that since the petitioners in the matter had almost finished their submissions, he was confident of wrapping up the hearing. items.title: Classic case of how not to investigate: Supreme Court slams UP Police again for botched murder probe
items.summary: The Supreme Court on Monday slammed the Uttar Pradesh Police for carrying out a slipshod and compromised probe in a murder case, terming it an egregious example of how a criminal inquiry should never be conducted [ Arun @ Deepak v. State of UP ]. A Bench of Justices JB Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran censured the State police for fabricating a case without basic investigative steps. "The State Police would do well to educate their officers in the process of investigation...Six years have been erased from the life of a man on the strength of a concocted story built on mere surmises and conjectures. Not even a rudimentary investigation was carried out...The investigation and prosecuting agencies exist not merely to, and by whatever means bring in a conviction," the Bench remarked. It observed that the botched investigation put an innocent citizen’s life and liberty into serious jeopardy. "This is a classic case of how an investigation should not be proceeded with, resulting in the prosecution putting into jeopardy a person’s life and liberty...We were appalled at the manner in which the investigation was carried out," the Bench noted. It directed the Uttar Pradesh government to pay ₹6 lakh in compensation to the accused, one Deepak, who spent six years as an undertrial behind bars. Justice JB Pardiwala and Justice Vinod Chandran The development comes amid repeated strictures passed by the apex court against the UP Police over botched and compromised investigations. Last month, a Bench led by Justice Sanjay Kumar had remarked that the Court might as well disband the State's police force and hand over all matters to the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), after flagging serious discrepancies and cover-ups in criminal inquiries. We might as well disband UP Police: Supreme Court on "cover up job", biased probe In the present case Deepak had approached the top court seeking bail after being in custody since November 2019 in connection with an FIR registered in Agra under Sections 364 ( kidnapping to murder ), 302 ( murder ), and 201 ( disappearance of evidence ) of the Indian Penal Code. Taking note of his prolonged custody in a case hinging entirely on circumstantial evidence, the Supreme Court in March this year directed the trial court to conclude proceedings within three months. items.title: Should farmers starve? Sharp exchange in Supreme Court between lawyers over  land acquisition for Ayodhya development
items.summary: The Supreme Court on Monday reserved its judgment on a plea challenging the acquisition of around 450 acres of land for a development scheme in Ayodhya. During the hearing, a bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant , Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Johanna observed that social impact assessment should not be brushed aside lightly, but cautioned against making it a “millstone around the neck” of the State. The hearing was also privy to sharp exchange of words between lawyers with those opposing the land acquisition flagging the impact it could have on farmers in the area. CJI Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi, Justice V Mohana The Court was hearing Shri Saryu Nagar Vikas Samiti’s challenge to an Allahabad High Court judgment concerning the acquisition of land under the Uttar Pradesh Awas Evam Vikas Parishad Adhiniyam, 1965. The High Court’s August 6 ruling declined to quash the acquisition but directed that landowners receive compensation, rehabilitation and resettlement benefits on the same parameters as the 2013 land acquisition law. It held that undoing the proceedings would jeopardise the public purpose, with some land already allotted to third parties. Before the Supreme Court, the Samiti argued that the 2013 law’s protections extend beyond compensation to safeguards governing acquisition itself, including social impact assessment and restrictions on acquiring irrigated multi-crop land. Senior Advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan submitted that two earlier schemes covered approximately 1,400 acres, of which only 70 acres had been utilised. He questioned the need to acquire another 450 acres without examining the availability of previously acquired land. Defending the acquisition, Additional Solicitor General Aishwarya Bhati said the third phase formed part of Ayodhya’s comprehensive development, including housing, roads, schools, hospitals, hotels, mutts and ashrams. Possession has been taken in three of four villages, she said. The submissions prompted a sharp exchange over construction of hotels in the city. “How can a place like Ayodhya have no hotels?” Bhati asked. “Do not take multi-crop land for it,” Sankaranarayanan responded. When Bhati referred to global attention on Ayodhya’s development and pilgrimage, he asked, “And so let the farmers starve?” “Nobody is starving anyone,” Bhati replied, maintaining that statutory compensation and other benefits were being provided. Noida-based Twisha Sharma had married Bhopal-based lawyer Samarth Singh after the two met through a dating app. Barely five months into the marriage, Sharma was found hanging at her matrimonial home in Bhopal on May 12. items.title: Depression after spouse's death sufficient ground to condone delay in consumer complaint: Delhi Commission
items.summary: The Delhi State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission recently held that depression following the death of a spouse can constitute sufficient cause for excusing delay in filing a consumer complaint [Priya Mehrotra v. Tata AIG General Insurance Co. Ltd.]. A Bench of Commission President Justice Sangita Dhingra Sehgal and Member Bimla Kumari made the observation while condoning a 250-day delay in a widow's complaint against Tata AIG General Insurance Company over the rejection of a medical insurance claim. The Commission accepted that the complainant's treatment for clinical depression following her husband's death sufficiently explained the delay. " On perusal of record, we find that there has been a delay of 250 days in filing the Complaint before the District Commission, for which, the Appellant has given sufficient cause, being that she was seeking treatment for clinical depression after the demise of her husband. Therefore, it would be in the interest of justice to condone the delay in filing the Complaint of the Appellant. Having condoned the delay, the District Commission is directed to decide the said Complaint on merits ." the Commission observed. The case arose after Priya Mehrotra's husband, Saurabh Mehrotra, a dentist, suddenly fell ill while working at his clinic on August 16, 2021. He was initially taken to Kukreja Hospital in Delhi and subsequently referred to Sir Ganga Ram Hospital. According to the complaint, initial investigations did not reveal serious abnormalities. However, his condition deteriorated, and doctors subsequently informed his family that his liver had suffered severe damage. He was later shifted to the Institute of Liver and Biliary Sciences, where he died on October 27, 2021. Mehrotra subsequently sought reimbursement of ₹25.73 lakh towards her husband's treatment under a Tata AIG health insurance policy. However, the insurer rejected the claim in January 2022, stating that treatment for cirrhosis fell within the policy's two-year waiting period. items.title: Peace bonds: The colonial tool rearing its head amid protests in 2026
items.summary: In 2023, the Indian parliament enacted three new penal laws: the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA), in place of its colonial era ancestors, a move that Union Home Minister Amit Shah said would make the criminal justice system "completely Swadeshi" . Back then, lawyers criticised the "new" statues as "old wine in a new bottle", largely retaining many problematic provisions introduced in colonial times. In 2026, the means adopted by the British Raj of quelling dissent still remain firmly cemented in Indian penal procedures. The recent nationwide protests and the police response to them put these provisions under the spotlight, especially those that deal with preventive policing. Detained protestors were made to sign bonds promising not to cause "breach of peace" for varying amounts of time. Here, we give historical context to these peace bonds, show how they have been retained in current jurisprudence and speak to leading criminal law practitioners on the issue. Medieval England and the colonial roots of peace bonds Over 600 years before the "swadeshi" laws were introduced, on the Sunday before the Feast of the Conversion of St Paul in 1361, King Edward III enacted the Justices of the Peace Act . This 14th-century legislation gave Justices of the Peace - the modern-day equivalents of magistrates - the statutory power to take sureties from people suspected of being threats to peace or of bad character, to secure their good behaviour. This statutory power of "binding over" was generally preventive in nature, not punitive. A few centuries later, with profound political and religious changes, the Justices became lynchpins of monarchs who, in turn, were able to advcance their policing power. Under Queen Elizabeth I , Justices of the Peace were given authority to enquire into all cases of persons accused of maintaining, defending, or extolling - by word or deed - the authority of the Pope in England. As time went by, every monarch and government used the Justices for two main tasks - the enforcement of the new order and the repression of dissent. Whenever political danger was apprehended, a more rigorous execution of the law could easily be brought about by issuing orders to the Justices. When the British Raj laid down its roots in India, it brought this apparatus with it. items.summary: A Bengaluru court has awarded nearly ₹3.78 crore in damages to a former Willis Towers Watson (WTW) employee after finding that his termination was retaliatory and breached the company’s obligation to protect whistleblowers [Naveen Kumar Midha Vs Rohit Jain]. By way of a judgment dated October 16, Additional City Civil and Sessions Judge Shirin Javeed Ansari partly allowed the suit filed by Naveen Kumar Midha, who had headed the company’s Health and Benefits business. The Court held that a contractual provision permitting termination upon notice or payment of salary could not, by itself, excuse a breach of the company’s commitment against retaliation for being a whistleblower. “ The contractual provision permitting termination upon notice or salary in lieu thereof does not, by itself, cure an exercise of that power which is inconsistent with the applicable non-retaliation commitment, ” the Court said. Midha alleged that he had raised concerns about fictitious transactions, phantom payments, questionable vendor payments and alleged sub-broking activities contrary to regulatory requirements. He relied on communications and meetings between July 2017 and July 2018 to establish that he had reported these concerns to senior personnel of the company. He was suspended on July 17, 2018. The suspension was revoked on September 27 but his employment was terminated the following day. The company disputed his claims and relied on the contractual termination provisions. They also pointed to his subsequent employment and remuneration to contest his claim for financial loss. The Court held that the notice clause and whistleblower protection operated in different spheres. One prescribed the mechanism for terminating employment, while the other governed the treatment of employees making protected disclosures. Both had to be read harmoniously. It was unnecessary to hold that the whistleblower policy had deleted or superseded the termination clause. The question was whether the termination power had been exercised contrary to an independently binding obligation against retaliation. “ The policy is not to be treated as a decorative or inconsequential document. items.summary: The Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh High Court recently ruled that consumer claims exceeding ₹50 lakh are maintainable before the J&K State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission if they were instituted before the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 came into force in the Union Territory [Tabeen Mineral Water Pvt. Ltd. V/s National Insurance Company Limited] A Division Bench of Chief Justice Dr. Pushpendra Singh Bhati and Justice Mohd Yousuf Wani asked the State Commission to re-adjudicate cases it had previously dismissed for lack of pecuniary jurisdiction. “All those cases in which the pecuniary limit is above Rupees Fifty lakhs shall be admissible and shall be required to be adjudicated on merits and any dismissal or non-interference on account of the upper pecuniary limit of Rupees Fifty lakhs is quashed, and such matters shall be required to be re-adjudicated by the Commission strictly in accordance with law and on their own merits,” the Court ordered. Chief Justice Dr. Pushpendra Singh Bhati and Justice Mohd Yousuf Wani The Court was hearing an appeal and a writ petition concerning consumer complaints filed before the State Consumer Commission. It was submitted that the Commission had dismissed the complaints, which sought compensation exceeding ₹50 lakh, solely on the ground that it lacked the pecuniary jurisdiction to entertain them. In the judgment passed on October 21, the Court examined the legislative history of Section 15 of the Jammu and Kashmir Consumer Protection Act, 1987. The law, which was replaced by the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, initially provided for a pecuniary limit of ₹50,000 to ₹10 lakh. In 1997, these limits were increased to ₹5 Lakh and ₹30 Lakh. The Court noted that a 1998 amendment omitted the upper pecuniary limit of ₹30 lakh. It added that a subsequent amendment in 2011 substituted the figures of ₹5 lakh and ₹30 lakh with ₹10 lakh and ₹50 lakh without addressing the earlier omission. The Court said this omission had led to a legislative anomaly as a person claiming compensation above ₹50 lakh was rendered remediless. It noted that the Commission had been following this position of no upper limit for a number of years until the High Court in Met Life India Insurance Company Ltd & Another v. items.title: Kerala High Court changes its internship policy; only those in final 2 years of LL.B allowed
items.summary: The Kerala High Court has revised its 2026 internship policy, introducing new rules governing applications, entry passes, attendance and the conduct of law students interning at the High Court. The revised policy, titled ' Internship Policy for the High Court of Kerala-2026 (Amended), ' was notified on October 17 and lays down detailed procedures governing internships at the High Court. Clause 6(a) of the policy states that "o nly students in the last two years of their law courses shall be eligible to undergo an internship in the High Court. " The restriction, however, does not apply to internships permitted at the discretion of judges. The policy applies to law students interning under High Court judges and other sections of the Court as well as offices including those of the Advocate General, Additional Solicitor General, Director General of Prosecution, Deputy Solicitor General, Kerala State Legal Services Authority, Mediation Centre, Bar Council of Kerala and other advocates. For internship opportunities under the judges, applications will be processed only after obtaining their consent. Under the new framework, students will be required to submit their internship applications through an online module, which will be developed by the High Court. Until the module becomes operational, applications and other internship-related procedures will continue to be handled online. The applications are to be forwarded through the principal or head of the institution where the student is studying. The Public Relations Officer (PRO) of the High Court will be responsible for overseeing the internship program, including processing applications and maintaining attendance records. Interns are prohibited from using mobile phones, cameras or recording devices inside courtrooms. Recording court proceedings in any manner or circulating it on social media to compromise the Court's security would lead to immediate termination of the internship, as per the policy. They are also required to maintain confidentiality and avoid disturbing court proceedings. The interns have to record their attendance daily and the actual number of days where they are physically present in the Court would be counted as the internship period for issuance of internship certificates. items.title: Legal Notes by Arvind Datar: Tea with 103-year-old Taraporevala
items.summary: On October 22, 2026, I had the privilege of having tea with 103-year-old Vicaji J. Taraporevala. I have known this centenarian for almost three decades but was meeting him after 20 years. I shall always be grateful to Justice Manoj Sanklecha, retired judge of the Bombay High Court, and Taraporevala’s former junior, for arranging this meeting. For some inexplicable reason, Justice Sanklecha’s number appeared on my phone’s screen on October 21. By a happy coincidence, I was to appear before the Bombay High Court the next day. I called him and enquired about Taraporevala. To my delight, I was told that he was fine. Justice Sanklecha agreed to fix an appointment the next evening. Justice Manoj Sanklecha, Vicaji J Taraporevala My mind went down memory lane. There was a case before the Customs and Excise Tribunal, and Taraporevala was unable to come down to Chennai. Sanklecha and I appeared and we succeeded. Thereafter, I remained in touch with Taraporevala for some time. Early days Vicaji Jivanji Taraporewala was born on June 21, 1923 and joined the chambers of the leading Sir Jamshedji Kanga in 1946. (Incidentally, Nani Palkhivala had joined the same chamber two years earlier). Over the years, Taraporevala practised before the Supreme Court, the Bombay High Court and, particularly, before the Central Excise, Customs and Service Tax Tribunal (CESTAT). Renowned author What set Taraporevala apart from other lawyers were his legal commentaries. Well before I had the opportunity of working with him, I had purchased his excellent commentary on the “Law of Central Excise”. This branch became an important area of practice in the late 70s as every manufactured product became liable to excise duty. In 1982, the Tribunal was formed with a Principal Bench in New Delhi and four regional benches. I had to often refer to Taraporevala’s commentary on this subject and was impressed with his explanation of the basic concepts of this levy. The success of this book encouraged him to write another commentary on “Customs law – Custom Levy, Valuation and Classification”. This too became an indispensable book for indirect tax practitioners. In 2005, my bookseller brought me a copy of Law of Intellectual Property. To my surprise, it was written by Taraporevala. This book was released when he was 82 years old, and its popularity called for two further editions in 2012 and 2019. items.title: State cannot deny compensation to rape victims for not producing medical report: Allahabad High Court
items.summary: The Allahabad High Court on Friday ruled that the State cannot deny financial assistance to rape victims for failing to produce an injury report indicating penetrative sexual assault in cases under Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act (POCSO Act). A bench of Justice Saral Srivastava and Justice Garima Prasad held that an injury report is not mandatory for receiving the financial assistance under the Uttar Pradesh Rani Lakshmi Bai Mahila Evam Bal Samman Kosh Rules, 2015. The Court therefore quashed a condition that made production of the medical examination report mandatory in cases of aggravated penetrative sexual assault. "Where a medical or injury report is available, it may be placed before and considered by the authority; its absence, however, cannot operate as an absolute bar to monetary relief. The impugned documentary condition is, accordingly, declared unconstitutional and is struck down," the Court ruled The rules provide for financial assistance to women and children who are victims of heinous and violent crimes, particularly sexual offences. However, one of the conditions require the victims of penetrative sexual assault to produce a copy of the FIR, the charge-sheet and an injury report indicating penetrative sexual assault. The Court said none of the three documents on their own constitute a judicial determination of the commission of the alleged offence, and the case is decided upon the totality of the evidence. It explained that even in a criminal trial, an accused cannot be acquitted merely because an injury report is absent or the available report does not record a penetrative injury. "It would, therefore, be anomalous to make the same report an absolute condition for preliminary monetary relief under a social-welfare scheme, particularly when the FIR discloses the offence and the investigation has resulted in a charge-sheet under the relevant provisions of the POCSO Act," the Court said. Justice Saral Srivastava and Justice Garima Prashad The availability of an injury report does not determine the seriousness of the allegation, the credibility of the victim or her need for monetary relief, the Court observed. items.title: Constitutional lawfare and why courts must stay away from political interest litigation
items.summary: Lawfare is a term that has increasingly been used since the turn of this century to describe the use or misuse of courts and legal institutions to achieve a desired political or military objective. The term has been employed to denote the use of law and legal systems against indigenous populations of the United States of America. It has also been used in the international military context to characterise/demonise legal actions brought against military actions of the USA and Israel. While a more traditional understanding of lawfare denotes powerful actors delegitimising the less powerful who are seeking rights and accountability, in India, lawfare could assume another dimension. A slew of recent such judicial actions would make this clearer. On October 5, the Punjab and Haryana High Court directed the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) to register a criminal case to probe corruption allegations involving Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann's office. What is noteworthy is that the order was passed on a public interest litigation (PIL) filed by advocate Nikhil Saraf. He told the Court that the Punjab Police had failed to take appropriate action on the letters written by the Enforcement Directorate (ED) for a probe into the allegations against Chief Minister Bhagwant Singh Mann's Officer on Special Duty (OSD) Rajbir Singh Ghuman. Whose investigation is it anyway? Under our Constitutional scheme, law and order is a State subject handled by the State Police. With a few exceptions, law and order matters, including those related to corruption, rests with State investigating agencies. The CBI usually comes in when Central government officers are involved in the offence or if a court calls for its interference. Lately, the ED, a central agency tasked with investigating money laundering offences, has been writing letters or making recommendations under Section 66 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) to State agencies to probe matters or register FIRs. The reason is not far-fetched. The ED comes into the picture only if there is an underlying predicate offence. Once the ED's jurisdiction kicks in, it can exercise vast powers including keeping an accused in jail as an undertrial prisoner without bail. items.title: Plea before Supreme Court seeks expert committee headed by former CJI to examine ECI's functioning
items.summary: A public interest litigation (PIL) petition has been filed before the Supreme Court seeking constitution of an independent expert committee, chaired by a former Chief Justice of India or a former judge of the top court, to examine institutional shortcomings in the functioning of the Election Commission of India (ECI). The plea, filed by advocate Vishal Tiwari, has also sought directions to the ECI to enforce an "absolute prohibition" on election campaigning using religious tags, religious symbols, communal appeals, sectarian identity or hate speech. The petition states that it is intended to be non-partisan and prospective and that the petitioner is not seeking a finding against any political party or office-holder, nor does it challenge the result of any election. It relies on a September 23 report by The Indian Express that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had recorded written objections on at least 14 occasions over ten months regarding unilateral decisions taken by Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. As per the petition, these objections pertained to unauthorized alterations to statutory Form 6, centralisation of the electoral database, unapproved appeal filings in West Bengal, and work allocation orders. The ECI, the plea says, acknowledged the dissenting notes but described them as routine suggestions, without clarifying who authorised the changes to Form 6. The plea has also flagged the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in West Bengal. Citing media reports of an ECI affidavit, it states that approximately 38.20 lakh appeals had been filed by persons excluded from electoral rolls of which only around 1.02 lakh have been disposed off. The ECI reportedly sought an increase in appellate tribunals from 19 to 42. Another report cited in the plea states that 2,70,313 electors in Maharashtra's draft electoral roll were shown as aged between 101 and 150 years due to a default birth year glitch. Hence, the ECI's shortcomings should be examined by a committee of experts. The proposed committee, as per the plea, should include experts in constitutional law, election administration, statistics, technology, cybersecurity and data protection. items.title: SEM notice asking Neha Bora to sign peace bond not based on mere hearsay: Delhi High Court
items.summary: The Delhi High Court on Friday observed that the show-cause notice issued by a Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) to All India Students Association (AISA) president Neha Bora to execute a personal bond of ₹10,000 and maintain peace was not based on mere "hearsay". Justice Subramonium Prasad observed that the notice was based on the kalandara dated October 17, which consists of the three general diary entries registered at different police stations related to different dates and events. "As such, this Court cannot sit in the armchair of the SEM to test the subjective satisfaction of the sufficiency of material and as to whether the opinion has been correctly been arrived at by the SEM or not," the Bench said. The Court said that the notice, issued under Sections 126 and 130 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), met the legal requirements for initiating preventive proceedings. The High Court arrived at these findings while dismissing Bora's plea against the notice. However, the Court directed the police to provide all the material to Bora on which reliance will be placed at the time of enquiry and on which basis the notice has been issued. "The SEM is also directed to ensure that the principles of natural justice are not violated before passing any order directing furnishing of a bond," the Court ordered. It clarified that the SEM must independently assess the material before deciding whether Bora should be directed to furnish a bond during the inquiry. "This Court, however, deems it fit to state that the SEM must necessarily keep in mind the import of Section 135 of the BNSS and leaves it open for the SEM to decide on the insistence of a bond at the first instance, as the provision provides for furnishing a bond only if there is an apprehension of breach of peace or disturbance after the commencement and before the completion of the enquiry," the Court said. Justice Subramonium Prasad The notice under challenge was issued by the Delhi Police to Bora on October 18, directing them to appear before the Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) on October 19. items.title: Life Insurance Guide for South Indians: How to Buy the Right Plan in 2026
items.summary: Buying life insurance in 2026 takes about as long as ordering groceries, which is both the good news and the trap. The purchase is easy; the decision still deserves care. This is a working guide for the urban South Indian professional who wants to get it right in one sitting: what to buy, in what order, and the five steps from decision to policy document. Step One: Decide the Job to Be Done Every life insurance product answers one of two needs. Income replacement if you die, which is protection. Or a disciplined pot of money if you live, which is saving. Protection is urgent and comparatively inexpensive; saving is important and has many competitors. So the sequence is fixed: a large pure term insurance cover on the earning member first, sized at 10 to 15 times annual income plus outstanding loans 1 , and only then any savings-oriented policy for named goals like education, a home or retirement. Step Two: Know the 2026 Advantages Two recent changes tilt the maths in the buyer’s favour. GST is not applicable on individual life insurance premiums, so a quoted premium is the amount you actually pay. And digital underwriting has matured, meaning salaried applicants with clean health records often complete everything, from quote to medical to issuance, without visiting a branch. Step Three: Shortlist on the Numbers That Matter Three filters do most of the work. The claim settlement ratio from the insurer’s public disclosures, which every insurer publishes annually under the regulator’s framework. The premium for your exact age, cover and term. And solvency and service signals, which in practice means how easily you can reach the insurer after the sale. Ignore brand advertising entirely; the disclosures tell you more than any billboard. ABSLI settled 98.86%* of individual death claims in FY 2025-26, as per annual audited figures submitted to IRDAI. Step Four: Configure, Then Declare Honestly Riders for critical illness and accidental death add meaningful protection for a small sum. A monthly income payout option suits families that have never managed a lump sum, and the plan allows between 10% and 90% of the sum assured to be taken as income over 10, 15 or 20 years. When planning for future goals, consider aligning the product with the investment horizon and risk appetite. Guaranteed savings plans may be suitable for goals that require greater certainty around outcomes, while market-linked plans such as ULIPs are generally designed for long-term wealth creation

items.title: Print, Scan and Copy: Does a College Student Need an All-in-One Printer?
items.summary: Your assignment is ready, but the print shop has closed. Tomorrow, you also need a copy of your college ID and a scanned signature for an internship application. These small jobs can make owning a printer tempting. But convenience alone does not settle the decision. Some students print every week; others submit almost everything online. An all-in-one printer for college students makes sense when printing, scanning and copying are regular needs. If they are rare, campus facilities and a phone scanner may be enough. What Does an All-in-One Printer Actually Do? An all-in-one printer combines three functions in one machine: ● It prints digital files, such as assignments, reading material and application forms. ● It scans paper documents into digital files for saving or uploading. ● It copies an existing paper document without requiring you to recreate it on a computer. You can therefore print a report, save a signed form as a PDF and photocopy a receipt using the same device. However, each function has limits. Printing a long document quickly does not mean the machine can scan a stack automatically. Start With Your Actual College Work Look at your previous month rather than imagining every possible use. Count printed pages, visits to the photocopy shop and documents you needed to scan. Also check hostel rules, available desk space and access to a plug socket before buying. Is a Scanner Better Than Your Phone? A phone scanning app can handle a readable receipt or a single signed page. Place the document in good light, keep the camera level and check the result before uploading. A flatbed scanner becomes useful when you want consistent page alignment, fewer shadows and clear copies of handwritten notes. You place the document on the glass and close the lid. It can also help with delicate originals that should not pass through rollers. Check the scanner's maximum document size. A printer that accepts longer paper does not necessarily scan that entire sheet on its glass. For several pages, a flatbed requires you to replace each sheet manually. An automatic document feeder handles a stack. Automatic duplex printing is a separate feature: it prints on both sides but does not automatically scan both sides. Choose Ink or Toner Around Your Subjects Colour matters when it carries information Architecture references, biology diagrams and presentation charts may lose meaning in greyscale. A colour inkjet is worth considering if these appear regularly in your coursework. F

items.title: Former Minister Anbil Mahesh arrested in alleged school approval scam
items.summary: Hours after the Madras High Court denied him anticipatory bail on Monday, October 26, former School Education Minister Anbil Mahesh Poyyamozhi was arrested by the Chennai police’s Central Crime Branch for his alleged involvement in collecting over Rs 100 crore from private school managements in the guise of “party funds” in exchange for government approvals. Justice V Lakshminarayanan passed the order earlier in the day, denying the former minister’s plea in the case being investigated by the CCB. The case centres on BT Arasakumar and Muthukumar, who claimed to be the founder-president and treasurer respectively of the Tamil Nadu Private Schools Association, an unregistered organisation. Arasakumar was a Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) spokesperson and Muthukumar is a former MLA, who is currently absconding. The duo were accused of collecting more than Rs 100 crore from private school managements by promising to secure permanent recognition from the government, school upgradation approvals, Directorate of Town and Country Planning (DTCP) clearances and other statutory permissions under the guise of “party funds” to the DMK, which was in power at the time. Arasakumar was arrested by the CCB on June 27 and subsequently detained under the Goondas Act on July 14. However, a special court in Chennai granted him bail on September 29 after the investigating agency failed to file its final report within the stipulated 90-day period. The investigation was later expanded to probe the involvement of Anbil Mahesh, who held the School Education portfolio during the time. On September 16, the CCB conducted searches at nine locations in Chennai and Trichy, including four premises linked to Anbil Mahesh and locations associated with his aides Valadi Karthik, Arun Prakash and Prakash. The former minister’s residence in Trichy’s Thennur was among the premises searched. On October 1, the Enforcement Directorate registered a case under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) in connection with the alleged racket. Its preliminary investigation is currently on tracing the money allegedly collected from private school managements and establishing how the funds were subsequently transferred or used.

items.title: Judge booked for letting minor son drive Mercedes that killed man in Kochi
items.summary: The Juvenile Justice Board in Ernakulam, on Monday, October 26, granted bail to the 17-year-old son of an Additional District Sessions Judge in connection with a fatal accident in Kochi that killed a scooterist in the early hours of Sunday. The judge has also been booked in connection with the accident, as the Mercedes-Benz sedan involved in the crash was registered in his name. According to police, he has been booked under section 199A(1) (holds the guardian or vehicle owner guilty for an offence committed by a juvenile) and 199A(2) (imposes criminal penalties on the guardian or owner, including up to 3 years' imprisonment and a Rs 25,000 fine) of the Motor Vehicles (MV) Act. The minor, who had initially been let go on station bail under Section 8 of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, was taken back into custody due to mounting public pressure and protests by the victim’s family. A Special Investigation Team (SIT) has also reportedly been formed to probe allegations made by the victim’s family. Fifty-five-year-old Jayabalakrishnan was killed in Ernakulam’s Cheranallur in the early hours of Sunday, October 25, after his scooter was struck by a car driven by the judge’s minor son. The accident occurred around 2.30 am when Jayabalakrishnan was going back home on his scooter after closing his street food stall. The speeding car rammed into his scooter from behind. The victim’s family alleged that the teenager attempted to flee the scene after the collision. However, the car stopped after a few metres due to the impact of the accident. An FIR has been registered under Sections 281 and 106(1) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita for rash driving and causing death due to negligence. Jayabalakrishnan’s family also alleged that undue influence was wielded by the judge’s family to shield the accused teenager. Jayalakshmi, Jayabalakrishnan’s niece, told the media on Sunday, “When I went to the police station, the SHO told me not to get emotional and that it was a 17-year-old who was involved. When I asked whether I could see him, they refused and also told me that he is the son of a district judge.” Speaking to the media, Jayalakshmi alleged that the minor’s father behaved arrogantly with her when she questioned the judge about allowing his underage, unlicensed son to drive. “I asked his father if he didn’t know that a 17-year-old cannot drive a vehicle. He replied arrogantly, ‘Don’t you dare to question me, you are not in a position to do that’,”
